analysis.one_liner: Extends overtime pay and minimum-wage protections to farmworkers.
analysis.headline: The bill gained 86 Democratic cosponsors in the House but never received a committee hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal law, farmworkers are excluded from the overtime rules that cover most other hourly workers, and many are also outside minimum-wage and maximum-hours protections. This bill would phase in overtime pay for agricultural workers after 55 hours a week in 2024, stepping down to 40 hours by 2027, with a later timeline for farms with 25 or fewer employees. It would also strip a series of exemptions that leave farmworkers outside the Fair Labor Standards Act's basic protections, ending the exclusion for non-family workers on small farms.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly two million farmworkers in the United States, many of whom are currently paid straight time no matter how many hours they work in a week. Under the bill they would earn time-and-a-half after long weeks, with the threshold starting at 55 hours and dropping to 40 hours over several years; farms with 25 or fewer employees would get a later start so they could adjust.

how_it_helps.text: Phases in overtime pay for agricultural workers: time-and-a-half after 55 hours beginning January 1, 2024, after 50 hours in 2025, after 45 hours in 2026, and after a standard 40-hour week in 2027 [S2].
Gives farms with 25 or fewer employees a later phase-in, so the overtime clock does not start for them until 2027 and the full 40-hour threshold does not apply until 2030 [S2].

Repeals the section of the Fair Labor Standards Act that treats agricultural workers differently on overtime and maximum hours, and narrows the small-farm exemption so it applies only to genuine family operations rather than to any hand-labor employer [S2].

Removes a set of exemptions that currently leave hired farmhands outside the law's minimum-wage, recordkeeping, and child-labor rules, and raises the coverage threshold for agricultural workers from 500 to 500 man-days as the operative small-farm test for related statutes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Farms and agricultural employers, who would pay time-and-a-half for long weeks or schedule fewer hours. Small farms with 25 or fewer workers would have the longest adjustment period. Some of the cost could show up in produce prices or in reduced hours for workers who want them.

drawbacks.text: The phase-in starts high: a 55-hour overtime threshold in the first year and 50 in the second means many workers would see little or no extra pay in the early years of the schedule [S2].

Growers could respond by cutting hours rather than paying time-and-a-half, so a worker who currently earns 60 hours of straight time might earn less total pay under a 40-hour cap, a cost an honest supporter has to weigh against the overtime guarantee.
Small farms with 25 or fewer employees would not reach the standard 40-hour threshold until 2030, leaving the workers on those farms without full overtime protection for years [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farmworkers, who are among the lowest-paid workers in the country and are currently excluded from overtime rules almost everyone else takes for granted, the gains are substantial: time-and-a-half for long weeks and, for many, minimum-wage and hours protections for the first time. The costs fall on growers, concentrated in labor-intensive crops, and the risk to workers is that employers cut hours instead of paying overtime. The multi-year phase-in and the carve-out for small farms ease the transition for growers but also delay the benefit for the people the bill is meant to help.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never took it up, so it died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raul Grijalva introduced the Fairness for Farm Workers Act on July 12, 2023, to extend overtime and other Fair Labor Standards Act protections to agricultural workers [S2].
86 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced [S1].
The full action history shows no further action: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm owners and agricultural employers are better off, because they continue to pay straight time for unlimited hours with no federal overtime obligation. Farmworkers gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Raul Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 86 cosponsors.

for.name: 86 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; the action history shows no action after the July 12, 2023 referral.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority controlling committee scheduling and the House floor
against.what_they_did: Controlled the chamber and its committees for the rest of the 118th Congress and never brought the bill to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 87 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; not a single House Republican signed on, and the Republican majority controlled both the committee and the floor for the rest of the Congress.

industries.note: The bill would require time-and-a-half after long weeks and bring hired farm labor under minimum-wage and hours rules, raising labor costs in a sector that has operated under a federal overtime exemption since 1938. The industry's savings from that exemption come directly out of farmworkers' pay for hours beyond 40.
Higher farm labor costs could raise wholesale produce prices, but the effect is indirect and modest compared with the direct effect on growers.
